originalGroup.material:
A Place in the Next Round

This original fictional case supplies all evidence needed for the questions.

A

The Hazel Park tennis club organised a small tournament for members with different experience. Its first announcement listed names and a date but left several practical questions unanswered. A player who saw an empty space in the draw thought she had won a match, while another assumed the first name on a sheet had chosen the earlier court. The organiser prepared a guide to the draw and schedule. The competition would still involve uncertain results; the guide’s job was to make the rules around those results understandable.

B

The draw showed how entrants would meet across rounds. A place in the next round could result from an actual match or from a stated bye where the draw required one. The guide distinguished these events rather than record every advancement as a played victory. The record could then explain why someone had reached a stage with fewer matches than another player. A blank opponent field was not left to carry an unexplained meaning. The draw and the match-result list described related but different parts of the competition.

C

Seeding followed the club’s published criteria before the draw. It placed selected entrants within the bracket under that arrangement; it was not a guarantee that they would win. The club kept a record of the criteria and date used, rather than reinterpret the seed numbers after results appeared. A player defeating a seed had not made the original label meaningless. The label described the role assigned at a stage of organisation, not a promise that future play would follow an administrative ranking.

D

The schedule assigned courts and times separately from the bracket. A name printed above another name did not automatically have the earlier arrival time. The club used clear match identifiers to connect the two sheets. Players were asked to check the current schedule, since a delayed match could affect the use of a court without changing which players should meet. The organiser did not redraw every relationship when a time moved. Identity of a contest and its place in the day were kept distinct.

E

Players reported availability before the schedule was finalised. The club could consider requests within the stated process, but a request did not become approval merely because it had been submitted. The final schedule identified what had actually been accepted. A player could ask about a difficulty rather than assume silence meant permission to arrive later. This distinction helped volunteers respond to a request and gave entrants a dependable record of the arrangement, instead of leaving each person to infer a private version from an earlier conversation.

F

The match format was stated before play: the competition’s particular scoring and completion rules applied throughout unless a defined change was announced. A result from another event using a different format was not automatically comparable by total games alone. The club named the format alongside results where this mattered. It did not assume every visitor knew the local arrangement from the general word tennis. A clear rule allowed players to focus on the contest without discovering a different expectation only when a match approached its end.

G

Rain caused one interruption. The organiser recorded the state of the match and the decision under the tournament’s procedure, rather than simply write cancelled. A suspended contest differed from one never started or one completed and reported. The record helped players and officials understand what remained to be done. The guide did not promise that the original time plan could survive every weather change. It made the status visible so a later update could be understood as a response to circumstances rather than a contradictory result.

H

Result entry included the match identifier and confirmation under the club’s process. A handwritten note with only a surname could point to the wrong contest if two members shared that name. The volunteer checked the draw and participants before entering it. If a score was corrected, the change history named the earlier entry and the basis for revision. A neat published table did not remove the possibility of an input mistake. It provided a public outcome that still needed an appropriate route for checking.

I

The event also offered a separate beginners’ session. Participation there did not place someone in the tournament bracket, and losing a tournament match did not automatically enrol someone in the session. The two activities had different purposes and registration arrangements. The guide described both without treating one as the compulsory route for everyone who had not advanced. Members could enjoy a competitive event and a learning activity in different ways. A result in one was not a complete account of what the club offered or what a person wanted from the day.

J

The published programme used photos only under the club’s agreed arrangements. A participant’s name in the result list did not automatically permit every use of a close portrait. The record separated competition entry from the proposed image uses and gave people a contact route for concerns. The club could report the competition without including unnecessary private details from registration. A public sporting result and an unrestricted personal profile were not treated as the same kind of information merely because they concerned the same member.

K

After the event, the club reviewed both the matches and the administration. A smooth final round did not show that the earlier instructions had been clear to new entrants. Volunteers recorded which questions had recurred and revised the guide for the next event. They kept the previous version dated so a returning player could see what had changed. The tournament had produced winners, but it had also produced evidence about its own procedure. Better organisation meant making the relevant distinctions easier to find before the next misunderstanding occurred.

originalGroup.material:
The Forecast Pinned by the Door

This original fictional case supplies all evidence needed for the questions.

A

A college outdoor club pinned a weather notice beside its meeting room. It showed a forecast icon and one temperature, copied from an online page the evening before. Members arriving in the morning assumed it described the day’s whole route. The trip leader noticed that the page referred to a town lower down the valley and covered a particular time. The club revised its notice procedure so a convenient summary would not appear to answer more questions than the source actually addressed.

B

The notice named the forecast location. A town report did not automatically describe every height and exposed point on a nearby route. The leader used the sources and planning arrangements relevant to the activity rather than treat a familiar place name as a guarantee of conditions everywhere around it. The record explained the area the information covered. This did not make local observations useless. It kept their geographical scope visible, especially when a brief icon made a large surrounding area look as though it shared one uniform condition.

C

The period was stated alongside the forecast. A symbol for an afternoon interval could differ from a whole-day summary, and a minimum temperature did not mean that value would persist all day. originalGroup.material:
The Triangle on the Plastic Cup

This original fictional case supplies all evidence needed for the questions.

A

A college environment group began a sorting campaign by putting coloured containers outside the dining hall. Members expected familiar symbols to explain the rest. The first inspection found that students interpreted the same mark in several ways and that a label on a product did not always match the collection service’s instructions. The group worked with the service to prepare a local guide. Its aim was to connect objects, actions and the actual destination of material, rather than assume that a more enthusiastic poster would resolve every uncertainty.

B

A material code on a plastic item identified information about its composition under the relevant system. It did not automatically mean the college’s collection service accepted that item. Shape, mixture and processing arrangements could matter as well. The guide separated the product mark from the local acceptance decision. A student could recognise the code correctly and still choose the wrong container if the code was treated as a universal disposal instruction. The poster named which source answered the composition question and which answered the local collection question.

C

The accepted list came from the college’s current collection arrangement. Another town’s leaflet might be informative but did not automatically describe the contract serving this campus. The guide included a date and a route for checking updates. It did not present local practice as a rule for every country or household. A change in a processor or collection agreement could require a new instruction even if the product looked identical. The relevant system was part of the meaning of accepted, not a detail that could be removed to make a simpler universal slogan.

D

One package was described as compostable under specified processing conditions. That did not establish it would break down in an ordinary garden pile or in any container labelled food waste. The service’s guidance determined whether it belonged in the campus route. The group kept the condition attached to the claim rather than repeat compostable as a complete instruction. A property assessed under one arrangement could be valuable while remaining different from a promise about every environment in which a consumer might place the object.

E

Mixed packaging needed a description of its parts. A container could include a lid or attached layer made from something different. The local guide showed which components the service expected to be separated where that rule applied. It did not infer one material for the whole object from the largest visible piece. The group avoided designing an instruction that required people to guess at hidden layers. Unclear examples were referred to the service, with the answer recorded for the next revision of the guide.

F

The service specified the relevant condition of accepted items, such as the state required before collection. The group repeated that instruction accurately rather than inventing a general rule that every object had to be washed in the same way. A sample photograph showed the state intended by this arrangement. The issue was whether the item met the route’s stated requirements. More effort by the student was not automatically more useful if it addressed a condition the service had not required or failed to address one it had.

G

An audit counted a described sample from named containers and times. Counts of objects and the mass of collected material were kept distinct. A large number of light cups could dominate one total without dominating the other. The report stated which quantity each percentage used. It did not announce that a change in one bin’s sample represented every campus building. The group wanted the audit to reveal practical problems, while preserving the boundaries of the observation that had produced its figures.

H

Collection was one stage rather than proof of completed recycling. The group asked what records the service could provide about later handling and reported the evidence available. A receipt showing pickup did not establish that every collected object had become new material. Some could be rejected during later sorting. The report distinguished the college’s action from claims about the whole chain. This made it possible to recognise participation without giving a collection photograph more authority than the process record could support.

I

The signs combined words, example shapes and colour. A student who could not distinguish two colours still needed a way to identify the route. The group tested the guide in the place where decisions occurred, including the size of labels and the examples visible at a normal distance. A clear image on a designer’s laptop was not the only check. The instruction also named where uncertain objects could be taken or discussed, so a gap in the examples did not become an invitation to choose a container at random.

J

A contaminated sample prompted a review of the sign and the collection process, not an immediate claim that all students were careless. The audit could show objects in a container, but not every person’s reason for placing them there. The group looked for recurring ambiguities and documented changes to the guide. It did not erase an inconvenient finding because a campaign had already been announced as successful. A useful report could recognise effort while asking which part of the system had made the wrong choice seem reasonable.

K

The revised campaign published a short, dated local guide and retained the reasoning behind its difficult examples. The group planned to check it when the service changed its arrangement. It avoided promising a permanent answer from a single colour or symbol. The work had become a connection between material identification, local processing, clear instructions and evidence about outcomes. That connection was more demanding than a universal slogan, but it gave students a dependable basis for the decision they actually had to make at the dining-hall containers.

originalGroup.material:
The Figure Behind the Screen

This original fictional case supplies all evidence needed for the questions.

A

A student arts group prepared a shadow performance for a community hall. The audience would see shapes on a screen while the performers worked behind it. The first rehearsal looked successful from the operating table, but a spectator at the side saw overlapping figures and missed part of a caption. The group began checking the performance from the audience’s positions. It needed an account of how light, objects, movement and written information reached viewers, rather than assume the arrangement looked the same from every place in the room.

B

A figure’s distance from the light and screen affected the size of its shadow. Making the cut-out itself larger was not the only way to change the projected shape. The group marked the intended positions and checked them during rehearsal. A performer moving forward could produce an unintended change in apparent size even while using the same object. The record connected a visible effect with the arrangement that produced it, so another operator could recreate the intended relation without relying only on the cut-out’s measured dimensions.

C

The screen view reversed some directions relative to the performers’ working view. An instruction to move left needed a stated reference. The director labelled movements by the audience’s view in the running notes and demonstrated the correspondence backstage. This avoided a sequence in which each performer interpreted left from a different position. The label did not change the physical stage. It made the shared direction clear enough that actions could be coordinated, especially where two figures were meant to meet rather than drift away from one another.

D

Overlapping cut-outs could create one combined shadow whose source was unclear. The group decided when this was an intended effect and when it hid an important action. A spectator could not be expected to reconstruct every object behind the screen. Operators therefore practised separation and timing in the relevant scene. The guide did not classify all overlap as an error. It named the intended relationship, allowing the team to distinguish an expressive merged shape from a moment in which the audience simply could not tell who had done what.

E

The captions had to remain visible from more than one seat. Testing only from the centre missed the side angle that cut off a word. The team adjusted position and size, then asked viewers to read the actual lines during the running scene. A static view of a clear title was not the same task. The captions appeared while figures moved, so viewers also needed enough time to divide attention. The rehearsal checked access in the situation where the information would actually be used.

F

Narration and captions did not always contain identical wording. A short caption could support understanding while a longer spoken line supplied detail. The group documented the relationship and checked that a person relying mainly on the text did not lose information essential to the plot. It did not assume that the presence of any words guaranteed equal access. The relevant question concerned what each route communicated. Where text had been shortened, the editor explained the choice rather than let missing meaning disappear behind the label captioned.

G

The sound cue list identified the point in the action at which each cue belonged. A file’s name alone did not give its exact entry time. The operator practised with the performers and recorded changes in the sequence. The group also kept a permitted backup arrangement for an unavailable cue. It did not assume every rehearsal recording authorised every later public use. Source and permission records remained connected with the selected version. The technical cue and the right to use the material were different requirements.

H

A performer could see a signal backstage that the audience could not. The director used this to coordinate transitions without expecting viewers to understand the hidden cue. The running notes distinguished visible story events from operating instructions. A pause while an object was changed could be designed as part of the scene or shortened if it merely exposed preparation. The team assessed the effect from the front rather than count every backstage movement as though the audience had witnessed it and understood its purpose.

I

Transport changed the positions of the portable screen and lighting equipment. The group checked the approved setup at the hall instead of relying on photographs from a smaller room. A clear shadow in one arrangement did not certify the same geometry elsewhere. The venue check also identified where performers and audience would move. The record described this production’s tested conditions under the responsible staff’s arrangements, not a general instruction for people to improvise unfamiliar lighting equipment from a drawing alone.

J

Feedback invited viewers to describe what they understood at specific moments. A comment that the show was enjoyable could not locate a missing caption or ambiguous action. The group retained both kinds of response for different purposes. It did not treat one confused spectator as proof the whole performance had failed, but a repeated misunderstanding prompted another look at the scene. The record named the moment and the evidence, allowing a revision to address a particular relationship instead of making every figure larger or every line louder.

K

The final rehearsal log linked cut-outs, positions, cues, captions and version dates. A replacement operator could follow the production’s choices without assuming every effect was a property of one object alone. The performance remained live and responsive, yet its important conditions were documented. The audience saw a simple story of moving shadows. Behind that simplicity was a set of relationships the group had learned to test: an object to its light, an operator’s direction to a viewer’s direction and a route of information to the person trying to follow it.

originalGroup.material:
The Name Looked the Same

This original fictional case supplies all evidence needed for the questions.

A

A fictional archive moved a multilingual name list between applications. Some names looked unchanged, some displayed an empty box and some could no longer be found through the old search. The team first treated these as one encoding problem. Investigation revealed several layers: stored bytes, character codes, displayed shapes and rules for comparison. A visible name could be useful without revealing all those layers. The archive documented them separately so that fixing a display problem would not silently change identity or erase an original spelling.

B

A file’s bytes needed the appropriate decoding rule to become the intended characters. Applying the wrong rule could produce readable but unintended symbols. The team recorded the encoding instead of guessing from a short fragment that happened to look familiar. A successful open operation did not prove the text had been interpreted correctly. The archive compared known examples and kept the original file available. Moving the bytes intact and understanding those bytes were different checks, both necessary to an account of what the transfer had preserved.

C

A visible character could involve more than one code point. An accented letter might be represented through a combined arrangement rather than the single code point another file used for a similar appearance. The team distinguished code points from grapheme clusters, the units a user could perceive as one written element under the relevant rules. It did not count every storage element as a separate visible letter. A matching appearance could conceal different internal sequences without making either sequence meaningless or automatically incorrect.

D

Normalisation could bring specified equivalent representations into a common form. The archive stated which normalisation it used and why. It did not assume every operation that made strings look simpler preserved every distinction. Compatibility transformations or other simplifications could change information relevant to a task. The team kept the original form alongside an appropriate comparison form. A useful equivalence rule was therefore explicit and bounded, rather than a promise that one general cleaning step could settle every question about textual meaning or identity.

E

Case handling was another decision. Converting upper- and lower-case forms involved a rule, not merely a universal visual operation. The archive checked the requirements of its languages and application. It did not assume that changing case was identical to canonical normalisation or that every change had the same effect in every context. A name used for display might need its supplied form retained even where a search function used a broader comparison. Different representations could serve related purposes without being interchangeable.

F

Ordering text was not the same as deciding identity. A collation could place accented forms close together for convenient browsing while the archive still retained distinct records. Likewise, removing a distinction in a search key did not authorise merging two people. The team documented the comparison purpose. A user could benefit from flexible discovery without the database pretending that every nearby or equivalent-looking result named the same person. The source record and the route used to find it remained separate parts of the system.

G

Length limits needed a unit. A field allowing a fixed number of bytes might hold different numbers of visible elements depending on the writing involved. Counting code points could also differ from counting user-perceived clusters. The archive named which limit applied and tested representative entries. A message saying a name was too long should not imply the person had supplied more visible letters than another user if the system was actually limiting a different storage quantity. The measurement belonged to an implementation rule that needed explanation.

H

Cursor and deletion behaviour exposed a related problem. Removing part of a combined written element could leave an unintended remainder. The editing interface was tested against the relevant cluster rules rather than treating every movement as one byte. This did not require users to understand the storage representation before typing. It required the application to support an intelligible editing task. A stored sequence could be valid while a poorly chosen boundary made ordinary editing confusing, especially when an invisible or combining element was separated from the character it modified.

I

Search used a prepared index, while display used the retained source form where appropriate. The archive recorded the transformations applied to the index. A broad match could help a user find a candidate, but it was not itself proof that two source strings were identical. Staff checked the underlying records before changing them. The arrangement preserved both access and evidence: people could search through variations without the system silently replacing every historical form with the one most convenient for an index.

J

An empty box on screen could indicate a missing glyph in the chosen font rather than missing data. The team checked the stored characters before concluding that a name had been lost. A fallback font could change spacing and line breaks while retaining the same character sequence. The display still needed assessment, but its appearance was not a direct inventory of the bytes present. Treating font coverage as an encoding deletion would lead the team to repair the wrong layer and might damage material that had remained intact.

K

A conversion into another encoding was tested for round-trip preservation where that was the requirement. A destination unable to represent a source character could replace it or report a problem. The archive preferred an explicit result over a silent substitution presented as exact. Recovering an output file did not prove every original distinction survived. The test connected the stated representation limits with actual retained information rather than assume that any successful export had the same preservation guarantee.

L

Some different character sequences produced very similar visible shapes. The team did not equate visual resemblance with identifier equality. In contexts where confusion mattered, it used an appropriate comparison and review process instead of relying on what a quick glance suggested. This was not a claim that all similar-looking names were suspicious. It recognised that appearance and internal identity answered different questions. A useful interface could help users notice relevant distinctions without forcing the storage layer to merge every form the screen made hard to distinguish.

M

File checksums could change after a documented normalisation even where a defined textual comparison treated the result as equivalent. Conversely, an unchanged checksum only showed that those bytes matched; it did not show a reader had decoded them correctly. The archive kept the relationship between raw and processed versions. The record made it possible to identify which representation an earlier tool had used. Preservation could include more than one form, provided their roles and transformations were visible rather than hidden behind a single current file.

N

The final policy depended on the task. Display, broad discovery and strict identifiers could need different comparison rules. The archive stated these choices and checked their consequences for the relevant users. It did not search for one universal equality that would make every application simple. A rule could be consistent and still unsuitable for a particular purpose. The review therefore asked not only whether the algorithm worked as specified, but whether the specification preserved the distinction the archive intended people to be able to make.

O

The corrected service retained original spellings, declared representations and documented routes between them. Some changes affected appearance, some comparison and some the actual information stored. The team could then explain what had been repaired and what had been left unchanged. A name looking familiar was no longer the final check. It was one piece of evidence within a layered account of text, where bytes, characters, clusters, glyphs and identity each had a role that could not be safely assigned to every other layer.

The archive preferred an explicit result over a silent substitution presented as exact. Recovering an output file did not prove every original distinction survived. In contexts where confusion mattered, it used an appropriate comparison and review process instead of relying on what a quick glance suggested. originalGroup.material:
The Result at the Next Look

This original fictional case supplies all evidence needed for the questions.

A

A fictional laboratory compared two procedures and watched incoming results. After one encouraging update, a manager wanted to stop and announce success. The analyst asked which stopping rule and interpretation the team had planned. Data could be inspected during a study for several purposes, but the consequences depended on the design. The team prepared an account distinguishing scheduled evaluation, quality checking and exploratory attention. The question was not whether looking at evidence was forbidden; it was which claim a particular sequence of looks could support.

B

An error-rate statement for one planned analysis with a fixed sample size did not automatically apply to an arbitrary series of repeated checks. Continuing until a favourable result appeared changed the process generating the reported result. The analyst therefore examined the whole decision rule, not only the final table. The report did not suggest that every repeated analysis was invalid. It identified the problem with borrowing a guarantee from a design different from the one actually followed, especially when earlier unfavourable looks were omitted from the account.

C

A stopping rule specified when observation would end or a decision would be made under stated conditions. Recording it only after a result appeared could conceal how the available data had influenced the choice. The team kept the planned rule and documented changes with their timing. An earlier stop might be justified, but its reason was part of interpretation. The procedure did not become equivalent to the original plan simply because the final sample size could be written as one neat number in the methods section.

D

Sequential designs could explicitly allow interim analyses. Their decision boundaries and interpretation were constructed for that arrangement. The laboratory considered such an approach rather than choose between never looking and looking without a rule. A planned interim result did not inherit its meaning from a standard fixed-look calculation used in a different way. The appropriate reasoning followed the design. This made monitoring possible while preserving an account of what the stopping decisions and resulting uncertainty statements were intended to mean.

E

Some monitoring concerned data quality. A broken measuring device or a missing stream could require action without being evidence that one procedure was better. The team separated checks of collection integrity from decisions based on the outcome comparison. This did not make quality checks magically independent of every result. It made their purpose and response explicit. The record described what had triggered a change, so a later reader could distinguish an equipment problem from a favourable effect that had prompted an early conclusion.

F

Group labels were sometimes concealed during preparatory work. That could reduce some opportunities for preference, but analysts might still see outcome patterns and make choices that depended on them. The team did not claim that a masked label prevented every data-dependent decision. It recorded which information was available and which steps were taken. A procedure could improve discipline without guaranteeing that all later choices had been determined before evidence was seen. The scope of masking mattered, not only the word printed in the report.

G

The chosen outcomes and analysis methods were also versioned. A justified amendment could improve a study, but a new question was not silently described as the one planned from the start. The record identified when it changed, what evidence had been available and why the team acted. This preserved the difference between a planned confirmatory claim and a later response to information. The laboratory did not treat all amendments as wrongdoing or all documented amendments as automatically harmless. It made their relevance available for examination.

H

Exploratory patterns could generate useful questions. The report labelled them as such rather than pretend they had all been predicted. A result found after examining many possibilities might warrant further investigation without carrying the same interpretation as a pre-specified test. The distinction did not reduce exploratory work to error. It connected a finding with the route by which it had been discovered. A later study could then examine the question under a suitable plan instead of repeating the origin story as though the new evidence were already present.

I

Planning the sample involved assumptions about variability, the effect of interest and the intended decision. A larger sample was not a general substitute for stating those aims. The analyst kept the planning assumptions separate from the effect estimated after data arrived. Using an observed favourable difference as if it had been known in advance could make the design look more inevitable than it was. The report named the original quantities and later estimates so readers could see which had guided the plan and which were results of carrying it out.

J

The team considered how many outcomes and comparisons it had examined. Selecting only the most favourable one could hide the opportunities for a striking result to appear. The account therefore described the relevant set and the handling appropriate to its claims. It did not say that many questions could never be investigated. It required the reported inference to reflect the search and decision process. A single final result did not become a single pre-planned opportunity merely because all the other analyses were left out of the publication.

K

An uncertainty interval had an interpretation under a stated procedure. Selecting the stopping point after repeated favourable looks could affect whether a familiar interval formula retained the guarantee readers expected. The analyst did not treat a narrow printed range as self-explanatory evidence of precision under any design. The report connected its interval method with the monitoring plan. The question was what the procedure supported, not whether the formatting contained brackets, decimal places and the familiar word confidence.

L

A separate assessment set could help examine a finding without reusing exactly the evidence that had shaped it. The separation had to be real for the purpose claimed. If the team repeatedly used that set to tune the method, it no longer played the same untouched role. The report named the information flow and the decisions it had influenced. Calling a file test data did not make it independent of development merely because it lived in a different folder or had been given a reassuring label.

M

A result that did not establish a difference was not automatically proof of equivalence. The relevant range and uncertainty mattered, and a design intended to assess practical similarity required its own defined question. The team retained those distinctions when discussing an early stop without a favourable result. It did not convert disappointment into a stronger conclusion than the data supported. A study could be informative about uncertainty or feasibility without settling every comparison through one of two dramatic words, success or failure.

N

The final account reported the planned and actual sequence, including relevant interim looks and changes. Readers could inspect how the published result had come to exist. This was more useful than a smooth description in which every decision appeared to precede the data. The record did not require publishing private information unrelated to the analysis. It required enough methodological context to distinguish a designed stopping process from an undocumented search for a favourable point at which to end the story.

O

The laboratory’s revised practice allowed monitoring with a clear purpose and an appropriate interpretation. It treated planning as a way to make choices examinable, not a promise that reality would never require change. Findings remained connected with what had been tested, seen and decided. A final statistic could then contribute evidence without borrowing an authority belonging to a different process. The report’s value lay in that connection between the procedure actually used and the claim now offered to the reader.

originalGroup.material:
The Short Line That Took Longer

This original fictional case supplies all evidence needed for the questions.

A

A fictional transport museum compared a geographical map with a simplified network diagram. Visitors often read a short printed link as a short or fast journey. The diagram’s designer had instead arranged lines to make connections legible. The exhibition asked what each mark represented and what information had been left to other layers. A map could be well designed for one purpose while unsuitable for another inference. The museum treated the diagram as a structured account of services, not a small photograph of every distance a traveller might encounter.

B

A station node could represent more than one entrance and several internal routes. Its dot was a convenient identity in the diagram, not an exact promise that every passenger began and ended at the same physical point. The exhibition linked detailed station information where needed. This mattered to someone comparing a street entrance, a platform and a transfer inside the station. The same name could connect these places institutionally without making their actual locations or the effort between them identical.

C

A drawn edge identified a connection under the diagram’s stated convention. Its printed length did not automatically measure the time or distance of the service. Two equally spaced stations could be far apart geographically, while a long-looking drawn link could represent a quick ride. The museum showed the convention beside the diagram. The mark remained useful when interpreted as a relationship, but it needed another source before supporting a different quantitative claim about the journey.

D

Geographical angles and spacing had been deliberately altered for readability. The design preserved selected connections while moving labels and simplifying bends. This was not necessarily a cartographic mistake. It was a choice about which properties mattered to the intended task. A traveller trying to walk between stations needed suitable geographical information rather than assume a straight printed link followed a straight street. The exhibition distinguished schematic distortion for legibility from an unsupported claim that the underlying city had the shape printed on the poster.

E

Services could be directional or operate only at stated times. An edge without that information could be misread as an option available in both directions throughout the day. The planning tool therefore connected the network with timetables and relevant service rules. The exhibition did not treat the poster as a live guarantee. Its representation described a stated version of a service arrangement. A route that existed in one period might not be available when a particular traveller wanted to depart, even though the station dots remained on the page.

F

A transfer was not free of time merely because two services met at one node. Platform movement, waiting, gates and other conditions could affect it. The museum used a detailed interchange example to show what the small connecting symbol compressed. A route with fewer train stops might still involve a demanding transfer. The point was not to make the diagram contain every corridor. It was to identify which further information a transfer decision required rather than let visual contact between lines stand for an effortless movement.

G

Shortest depended on the quantity being minimised. The fewest links, the lowest expected time and the smallest fare could favour different routes. A planning result needed its objective stated. The tool did not become universally correct by finding an optimal path under one cost function. It solved the defined problem using the supplied data. The exhibition asked visitors to compare two stated objectives rather than argue about the shortest route as if that phrase had one meaning independent of the person’s purpose.

H

A planned closure changed the available service graph without necessarily changing the geographical track. The system kept route information and current availability linked through dated updates. A familiar printed line could remain in a historical or general diagram while not being usable in the current plan. The tool identified the version and notices considered. A route recommendation could then be examined against the information available at the time, rather than judged as if every diagram had always contained every live change.

I

Waiting time involved a model as well as a timetable. An expected interval under stated conditions was not a promise of the exact wait for the next passenger. The exhibition explained the assumptions used in its example rather than present one average as every person’s experience. The actual departure pattern could differ across periods. The museum kept scheduled service, observed service and an expectation derived from them recognisably distinct. Each could help a planning question without replacing every other account of time.

J

Capacity and congestion could matter too. A theoretically available service might be difficult to board under a particular load. The planning example stated whether these conditions were included or outside its scope. Omitting them did not make the diagram meaningless, but it limited which claim the output could support. A connected path in a simplified graph was evidence of a represented route, not an assurance that every traveller would complete it under every possible condition. The model’s boundaries were part of its interpretation.

K

Access requirements changed feasible paths for some travellers. A route involving steps could be unsuitable for someone needing a step-free option even when it had the shortest nominal time. The tool allowed the relevant requirement to be stated and relied on appropriate facility information. The exhibition did not treat all users as interchangeable points moving along lines. It showed how a condition could remove an option from one person’s problem without removing the physical service from the city or denying its usefulness to others.

L

A recommended route was linked to the assumptions and data used. If a necessary connection was missing from the database, the algorithm could not use it merely because it existed in the world. Conversely, a represented connection could be out of date. The system provided a route for reporting such issues. The museum separated a computational result under a graph from a complete claim about the city. A correct calculation on incomplete information could still produce an unsuitable answer for the actual trip.

M

Names supported discovery but could be ambiguous. Several stops shared a familiar place word, and an old name might remain in a guide after a change. The tool used stable identities and clear descriptions in addition to labels. A search result could offer a candidate without establishing that the user had selected the intended place. The exhibition connected naming with the represented object, rather than assume that matching the first familiar string settled every question about the start, destination or transfer involved.

N

Absence from a diagram had to be interpreted through its scope. A map showing one operator’s services might omit another available mode. That omission was not proof no route existed. The exhibition labelled the coverage and distinguished a service absent from the published layer from one known not to operate under stated conditions. A clean visual field could otherwise make a limited catalogue look like the entire travel world. The map’s usefulness increased when its omissions could be understood rather than silently filled by a reader’s assumptions.

O

The final display offered several coordinated views instead of one supposedly complete picture. Visitors could inspect network relationships, geography, service timing and relevant access details. The additional views did not imply the simplified diagram had failed. They explained what it was good at and which questions belonged elsewhere. A route became meaningful through a connection among representation, objective and traveller, not from the apparent authority of the shortest line on a neatly drawn poster.

originalGroup.material:
The Story Collected Twice

This original fictional case supplies all evidence needed for the questions.

A

A fictional folklore archive held two recordings of a story told by the same performer on different evenings. Their plots were recognisably related, but wording, pace and some details differed. A catalogue assistant first proposed choosing the more polished recording as the authentic text and treating the other as an imperfect copy. The project team instead asked what each recording preserved: an event, a version and a relationship with a particular audience. The archive needed a way to describe those layers without pretending that a living performance had always existed as one fixed page.

B

The telling event was distinct from a general story pattern. A recording captured a particular occasion, not every possible performance of the tale. The same plot could be told at another pace or with an added episode while remaining related under the project’s classification. The archive identified the event, performer and context rather than use one title to stand for all of them. The point was to preserve a connection without making every difference either a new unrelated work or an error measured against the chosen recording.

C

Transcription introduced divisions that speech had not necessarily marked in the same way. Paragraphs and punctuation made a page readable but could guide interpretation of a pause or a change of voice. The team stated its transcription conventions and kept the link to the recording. It did not treat the neat printed paragraph as evidence that the performer had spoken in that exact written structure. A text could aid study while remaining an edited representation, with choices another researcher might reasonably examine or revise.

D

Translation created another account. A familiar term in the target language could suggest a relationship or social category different from the one in the telling. The project retained selected source expressions with explanations and identified whose account supported them. It did not promise that one translation covered every use of the word across all communities. The aim was a route into this performance rather than an invented universal dictionary. Where alternatives remained, the notes made them visible instead of turning editorial convenience into apparent certainty.

E

Variation could respond to the audience and occasion. A performer might explain a reference for newcomers or shorten a passage for listeners already familiar with it. The team did not label every change as corruption of a stable original. It described the comparison and its evidence. The two recordings could reveal how a telling worked in context without establishing which form had existed first in the history of the tradition. The oldest surviving file was not automatically the first time anyone had ever told that story.

F

The collector’s questions were part of some sessions. A request to explain an unfamiliar action could interrupt the flow or invite a detail absent from another recording. The archive retained relevant prompts rather than edit them out and call the result entirely spontaneous. This did not make the telling inauthentic simply because a collector had participated. It made the circumstances of production visible. A researcher could then distinguish an unsolicited passage from one developed in response to a particular question, without assuming the difference proved one was more truthful.

G

Gesture and audience response could carry meaning not fully captured by a plain text. Laughter might follow an action rather than a word. Silence could be part of timing, not merely missing content. The project described the available record and its limits. A sound recording might preserve a response while failing to show the movement that prompted it. The transcript did not convert that limitation into proof no movement had occurred. Different media offered evidence of different aspects of the same event.

H

Permissions were documented for the particular recording and proposed uses under the project’s agreement. A person’s participation did not automatically authorise every later presentation, and one individual’s account did not settle every community’s view of shared knowledge. The archive consulted the relevant parties through its stated process. This was a responsibility of this collaboration, not a claim that one consent form could solve all questions of representation. The record named the scope so a later user could understand which use had been agreed and which needed further attention.

I

A collector’s label for the performer was kept distinct from the person’s own description. An old catalogue could use a role or group name that the performer had not supplied. The revision retained the historical wording as part of the record while identifying its source. It did not silently attribute every archive description to the person recorded. A label could be evidence about collection practice as well as an aid to finding a recording. Preserving that distinction allowed both the telling and its later institutional history to be studied.

J

The database used motif codes to support comparison. Two stories sharing a coded episode did not necessarily descend directly from one another. A resemblance could suggest a question without establishing a route of transmission. The team linked codes with passages and explained how it had applied them. A classification was a designed index, not a substitute for the whole performance. Its usefulness depended on knowing what counted as a match and what wider claim the code was not intended to prove.

K

Dates referred to different events. The recording date, publication date and date of an event remembered inside a story were not interchangeable. The archive gave separate fields where information was available and marked uncertainty. A later upload could make an old recording newly accessible without making it a new performance. The chronological account supported questions about circulation and collection while avoiding false precision. A familiar year on a catalogue page needed its role identified before it could become evidence for when a particular telling or remembered occurrence took place.

L

An unclear section in the recording was not filled with an invented word presented as certain. The transcript marked the uncertainty under its conventions and documented a proposed reading where appropriate. A later interpretation could then be checked against the source. Editorial brackets belonged to the new representation unless evidence showed they were original spoken material, which would be a different claim. The project separated what could be heard, what was proposed and what remained unresolved instead of making fluency on the page the final judge of the evidence.

M

A contemporary retelling for a school event was credited as a new performance drawing on the archive. It was not advertised as the untouched recovery of the earlier evening. The new performer made choices about pace, explanation and audience. Those choices could be artistically valuable while needing their own attribution. The archive linked the retelling to its sources and retained the distinction between the earlier records and the new contribution. Continuity of a tradition did not require pretending that every later participant was merely a device replaying the same fixed object.

N

Public access was managed according to the stated use arrangements. A web page could describe a recording even where the full file required a further process. The project did not treat discoverability as unrestricted use. It also explained what it could change on its own services if a later concern arose, without promising control of every copy already outside them. The access record preserved responsibilities and limitations rather than allow a convenient technical possibility to stand for permission that had never been obtained.

O

The completed catalogue offered recordings, transcripts, translations and attributed interpretations with routes between them. No single form was called the whole tradition. The archive’s contribution lay in making particular encounters available for study while preserving how each had been produced. It could value differences instead of ranking every version by closeness to an imagined original that the evidence had not established. The story remained something people had done with language, bodies and audiences, and the record became stronger when it kept those relationships visible.
